Denarius
di-NAIR-ee-uhs
noun
Latin denarius, the Roman silver coin worth ten asses; the “penny” of the Authorized Version; Greek dēnarion.

Biblical Definition

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin of the New Testament era, worth a day’s wage for a common laborer, and it is the coin the Authorized Version renders “penny”—a value far greater than the modern word suggests. It figures in some of the most familiar scenes of the Gospels. In the parable of the laborers in the vineyard the householder agrees with the workers for a penny a day, and gives the same penny to those who came at the eleventh hour as to those who bore the burden and heat of the day—a picture of the sovereign freedom of grace. When the Pharisees seek to entangle the Lord over tribute, He asks for a penny, points to Caesar’s image and superscription upon it, and answers, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. Two hundred pennyworth of bread would not feed the five thousand; and the good Samaritan left two pence with the host to care for the wounded man. The dictionary records the denarius as the day-wage coin of the New Testament, and notes that knowing its worth opens these passages: the equal penny that magnifies the freeness of grace, the tribute penny that orders the believer’s duty to the magistrate and to God, and the two pence of mercy shown to a stranger.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Roman silver coin worth a day’s wage, the “penny” of the Authorized Version; the coin of the vineyard parable, the tribute to Caesar, and the good Samaritan’s mercy.

The wage in the parable of the laborers in the vineyard.

Key Scripture

Mat 20:2 — "And when he had agreed with the labourers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard."

Mat 22:19 — "Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny."

Mar 6:37 — "He answered and said unto them, Give ye them to eat. And they say unto him, Shall we go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread, and give them to eat?"

Luk 10:35 — "And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the KJV “penny” misleads the modern reader; the denarius was a full day’s wage, and knowing this opens the parables.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The point to recover is one of understanding rather than corruption: the Authorized Version’s “penny” misleads the modern ear, suggesting a trifling sum, when the denarius was a full day’s wage for a laborer. To miss this is to miss the force of the passages. The eleventh-hour worker receives a whole day’s pay—a generosity that scandalizes those who bore the heat of the day and magnifies the sovereign freedom of grace, which gives to the late-come the same as to the early. The tribute penny is no token but the real coin of Roman taxation, and the Lord’s answer over it orders the whole question of the believer’s duty to the state.

The principle to recover is the doctrine carried by the coin. The equal penny in the vineyard teaches that God may do what He will with His own, and that grace is His to give freely—the last shall be first. The tribute penny, stamped with Caesar’s image, teaches that the magistrate has his due and God His: render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s. And the Samaritan’s two pence teach that true neighbor-love spends real cost to care for the stranger. The day-wage coin is a small window into great truths.
